title: Buried abuse memory brought sisters' half-brother to justice

input.lead: Mellissa Arkwright could not remember the abuse she suffered as a child until she had taking therapy
input.summary: Mellissa Arkwright could not remember the abuse she suffered as a child until she had taking therapy
input.evidence_text: Buried abuse memory brought sisters' half-brother to justice - BBC News Image source, Family photo Image caption, Nikita Dallison and Mellissa Arkwright have waived their right to anonymity to share what happen to them By Lauren Hirst North West Published 1 hour ago Sisters Nikita Dallison and Mellissa Arkwright were just six and seven years old when they began to be abused by their half-brother Adrian Austin. But while Nikita, 36, can remember the harrowing details vividly, Mellissa, 35, had no recollection of what happen to her as a little girl. It was only when Nikita bravely reported the abuse to police in 2021 that Mellissa decided to have a type of talking therapy known as eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing (EMDR). This involves listening to sounds, tapping, or flashing lights to remember a traumatic event. "I needed therapy because my mental health had spiralled way out of control... but I never understood why," said Mellissa. "It's horrific when you have it, because you feel every single sensation. "You can feel the atmosphere in the room when you're having that therapy." It unlocked a specific memory that would prove to be a crucial part of the evidence that brought their half-brother to justice. Austin, now aged 45, was jailed for 17 years in July after being found guilty of six counts of sexual intercourse with a girl under 13, which would be classed as rape under current sexual offences legislation. He was also convicted of four counts of indecent assault and one count of indecency of a child between 1997 and 2001. "It's still upsetting thinking about that day [when he was found guilty] because we got justice for those little girls," said Mellissa. title: Cancer survivor shares heartbreaking reality of surgical menopause

input.lead: An ovarian cancer survivor is backing Manchester Cancer Research Centre's study into new treatments
input.summary: An ovarian cancer survivor is backing Manchester Cancer Research Centre's study into new treatments
input.evidence_text: A cancer survivor who always dreamed of having children has opened up about the heartbreaking reality of going into surgical menopause at the age of 34 Gemma Coleman, who was diagnosed with two separate cancers affecting her ovary and womb in 2022, was told she would never be able to become pregnant after needing two major operations The 37-year-old, from Turton, Lancashire, said her diagnosis had "felt like a death sentence, but surviving cancer isn't the end of the story" as she now hopes to adopt in the future "You have to learn to live with the long-term physical and emotional impact of treatment," she said Gemma underwent two major operations, including the removal of her ovaries, womb, fallopian tubes, lymph nodes and affected abdominal tissue, followed by eight months of chemotherapy Now three years into remission, Gemma has regular scans and blood tests while managing the long-term effects of treatment including chronic pain, fatigue, bone weakness and fibrosis

title: Manchester couple begin round-the-world cycling challenge for Parkinson's disease

input.lead: The challenge was inspired by Ciaran Booth's mother, who has Parkinson's disease
input.summary: The challenge was inspired by Ciaran Booth's mother, who has Parkinson's disease
input.evidence_text: Manchester couple begin round-the-world cycling challenge for Parkinson's disease - BBC News Image caption, Lucy Pickersgill and Ciaran Booth plan to cycle about 18,000 miles through 30 countries By Kaya Black , Reporting from Greater Manchester and Haider Saleem , North West Published 9 August 2026 A former professional rugby player, who represented Ireland at under-20 level, has begun an 18,000-mile (30,000km) cycle around the world to raise £50,000 for charity. Ciaran Booth and his girlfriend Lucy Pickersgill, both 26, set off from Manchester Rugby Club in Stockport and plan to travel through about 30 countries over 18 months. The challenge was inspired by Ciaran's mother, Annie Booth, who has Parkinson's disease , external , and said sport and exercise had helped her both physically and mentally. Annie said she was "really proud" of the couple and described their journey as "shining a light on what's possible" for people living with the condition. Ciaran said his mother had found "loads of strength in community through sport" following her diagnosis, including through the charity Sport Parkinson's. He said Sport Parkinson's encouraged people with the condition to exercise and find support through a community. 'Get fit on the job' Despite Ciaran's background in professional sport, the pair describe themselves as beginner cyclists. Lucy had only begun cycling seriously in the months leading up to the trip, with the couple expecting to average about 100km (62 miles) a day. "You can't really train for something like that," she said. Ciaran said they planned to "get fit on the job" as they travelled through Europe before continuing towards India, Nepal and China, then South East Asia, Australia and New Zealand, followed by Canada and the US. Image source, Ciaran Booth Im

title: Trains returning to normal after Manchester power disruption

input.lead: Rail services were returning to normal after an outage in Manchester on Thursday caused major disruption
input.summary: Rail services were returning to normal after an outage in Manchester on Thursday caused major disruption
input.evidence_text: The rail network across northern England has been returning to normal after a power cut led to major disruption for thousands of passengers While the power was only down for 90 seconds at about 13:40 BST on Thursday, the delay to back-up systems at Network Rail's Manchester Rail Operating Centre meant trains had to stop running Many services were cancelled and commuters faced "nightmare" diversions Network Rail said services had "largely been restored across the North West", but some disruption to TransPennine Express services remained while trains and crews returned to their usual positions Network Rail's route director for the North West, Chris Wright, said: "We're continuing to work closely with train operators to return services to normal as quickly as possible." Manchester Rail Operating Centre was opened in July 2014

title: How a 90-second power outage sparked chaos for train commuters

input.lead: The incident raised questions about how a disrupted power supply can have such a widespread impact
input.summary: The incident raised questions about how a disrupted power supply can have such a widespread impact
input.evidence_text: But after commuters were left facing chaos , it has raised questions about how a short outage at one operating centre could have a widespread impact Network Rail will face scrutiny for how its systems coped and responded to the outage That's the publicly-owned body whose job it is to operate and maintain Britain's railway infrastructure. That means the tracks, signals, embankments and major stations It was at Network Rail's operating centre in Manchester that the problem started. Its operating centres are where crucial controls are housed that let trains run safely across the country, with Manchester's centre responsible for large parts of the North West It was hit by a power cut in the area, which was resolved within 90 seconds. Given the centre's importance, backups are in place. But questions have been raised about how they responded Chris Wright, north-west route director at Network Rail , told the BBC "we didn't experience a 90-second interruption," insisting its systems were back online sooner

input.evidence_text: Astronomy The best places to view the Solar Eclipse in Greater Manchester this week The 2026 partial solar eclipse is coming - and here's how to see it from in and around Manchester Comments News Bethan Finighan Science and Innovation Writer 06:00, 10 Sky watchers in the UK are gearing up for a spectacular partial solar eclipse this week As the Moon passes between the Sun and the Earth on Wednesday (August 12), up to 96 per cent of the Sun will be covered, dimming the sky as sunlight is blocked The solar eclipse will be visible across the whole of the UK. While those watching in the South West are likely to see the best eclipse, around 90 per cent of the Sun will still be covered from here in Greater Manchester In Manchester, the spectacle will begin at 6.13pm and end at 8.03pm, with the maximum eclipse at 7.10pm The best place to see the solar eclipse is anywhere with a clear view of the western horizon. It's also vital that anyone planning to witness the spectacle does not look directly at the Sun at any point during the event

input.evidence_text: Wigan Giant 'cruise liner' warehouses make life 'hell' for neighbours with relentless HGV noise 'The people who live bordering the warehouses are going through hell because of the noise' News James Connolly 20:37, 09 Aug 2026 View 3 Images John Peters Families living next to four giant 'monster warehouses' say their lives are now being made hell by relentless noise and traffic Construction of the four 60ft units hit the headlines last year with nearby residents saying their homes would be blighted by the massive buildings. Now the units have been completed and with one becoming fully operational residents say their lives are being ruined by constant HG The enormous grey sheds at Astley Business Park in Tyldesley, Wigan , lie just metres from some gardens. One of the four units is already operating - with neighbours claiming its round-the-clock logistics operation is shattering their peace John Peters, 71, said: "The people who live bordering the warehouses are going through hell because of the noise. The extent of the warehouse operations have been a real shock to the system and that's on top of the visual problem."
